# Apple Application Inventory Projection

REA can project one or more authenticated `inventory_artifact` Evidence records
for the same IPA, macOS `.app` directory, ZIP, or DMG into an Apple application
inventory. The projection is execution-free: it reports exact paths, content
hashes, detected formats, bundle anatomy, runtime-family hints, and path-based
bridge hypotheses. It does not parse plist or CMS semantics or claim observed
runtime calls.

Framework hints match complete path segments such as `React.framework`,
`ReactNative.framework`, `hermes.framework`, `Flutter.framework`, and
`UnityFramework.framework`. Substrings in `Preact.framework`,
`Community.framework`, or `MyApp.framework` do not identify those families.
A generic `App.framework` also does not identify Flutter by itself. Runtime
families remain inventory-derived hints, not observed loading. Generic framework
and dylib paths do not establish Swift or Objective-C; this projection does not
decode language metadata. A bridge basis is inferred from the native path and
repeated for each paired script, rather than proving a particular binding.

```sh
rea project-apple-application-graph '{"inventory_evidence":[<inventory_artifact Evidence>]}'
```

```json
{
  "name": "project_apple_application_graph",
  "arguments": {
    "inventory_evidence": ["<inventory_artifact Evidence>"]
  }
}
```

The result includes every component in each inventory category. Bridge
hypotheses are the path-based JavaScript/native pairs within each application
root. To keep their Cartesian expansion bounded, the projection limits the
serialized candidate array to 2 MiB. It computes the pair count and
exact UTF-8 JSON size before creating candidate objects, then retains a
deterministic prefix when the byte budget is exceeded. The result's
`bridge_candidate_coverage` reports total, emitted, and omitted pair counts;
overall coverage becomes `partial` and a limitation explains the omission.
Duplicate inventory pages are merged by artifact identity and occurrence path;
their Evidence IDs remain attached as source Evidence.

Content nodes identify bytes by SHA-256 and report only content-derived formats.
Each occurrence reports its own `artifact_kind`, `artifact_format`, and executable
permission. Identical bytes can therefore appear as a script, resource, or native
addon at different paths without overwriting another occurrence's role. Package
formats such as APK and IPA belong to the occurrence; their ZIP bytes share a
content format. Graph and directory identities use locale-independent Unicode
ordering.

For IPA inventories, archive components outside every application root remain
in the component lists. Their JavaScript and native candidates are grouped with
other unrooted components, preserving the inventory projection's path pairing
semantics without attributing them to an application bundle.

Coverage is `complete-within-inventory` when the supplied pages reconstruct the
complete authenticated inventory, and `partial` otherwise. A partial result
states that absence is unknown. Component arrays remain complete when candidate
hypotheses are omitted; component arrays still include every component from
the supplied inventory pages, and overall coverage is `partial` in that case.

Inventoried files whose bytes were not read, such as encrypted archive members,
are listed in `unavailable_components` with their original path, format,
encryption flag, limitations, and null content identity. The same application-root
and AppleDouble attribution rules apply. These files make overall coverage
`partial`; component absence is unknown even when `inventory_complete` is true.
Directories have no file bytes and symlinks remain in `symlinks`, so neither is
an unavailable file component. The additive field participates in `projection_id`,
including when empty, so Apple projection identifiers change.

## Application roots

| Inventory root                         | Application root                                    |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| IPA                                    | Each `Payload/<Name>.app`                           |
| `.app` directory                       | `.`, the inventoried bundle itself                  |
| Directory, ZIP, or DMG containing apps | Each outermost `<Name>.app` followed by `Contents/` |

File and slice occurrences supply component endpoints. Directory tree identities
remain in source inventory and bundle anatomy, and links remain in `symlinks`.

Root and layout discovery use known directories and ancestors implied by deeper
inventory paths. A leaf file or symlink named `*.app`, `Contents`, or `Versions`
does not establish that directory. Directory and authenticated-file identity are
selected before applying anatomy case preferences, so a file cannot shadow a
folded directory name or a directory shadow a metadata/signature file.

ZIP archives made with `ditto -c -k --keepParent` report `<Name>.app`. A DMG
reports `<image>.dmg/<Volume>/<Name>.app`; DMG child inventory needs the native
macOS mounting adapter. When a DMG has only its root identity, the projection is
`partial` and says that bundle absence is unknown. Other inventory formats, such
as APK or ASAR, are rejected as input errors.

An inventoried directory whose name ends in `.app` is its own root even when its
inventory is partial or lacks `Contents/`. For directory, ZIP, and DMG
inventories, components outside every application root are not attributed to
the application. This covers installers, disk-image extras, and AppleDouble
sidecars, which therefore stay out of runtime families and bridge candidates. A
limitation reports how many inventoried entries were left out. IPA projection
still lists every archive component, including `SwiftSupport/`.

`platforms` lists `macos` for application roots with `Contents/`. It lists `ios`
for shallow application roots that have an `Info.plist`. An application root
with neither, such as an empty inventory, has no platform.

## macOS bundle anatomy

`bundles` lists each application root and every nested bundle under it. Each
bundle reports its `parent_path`, `layout`, `info_plist_path`,
`executable_candidates`, and `signing_paths`.

| Layout                | Meaning         | Content directory                             |
| --------------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `macos-deep`          | Has `Contents/` | `Contents/`, executables in `Contents/MacOS/` |
| `versioned-framework` | Has `Versions/` | Each real `Versions/<version>/`               |
| `shallow`             | Neither         | The bundle directory itself                   |

Roles are path conventions (`role_basis: "path-convention"`):

| Role                 | Path                                                            |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `app-extension`      | `*.appex`                                                       |
| `xpc-service`        | `*.xpc`, including XPC services inside frameworks               |
| `framework`          | `*.framework`                                                   |
| `system-extension`   | `*.systemextension`                                             |
| `driver-extension`   | `*.dext`                                                        |
| `plug-in`            | `PlugIns/*.bundle`, `*.plugin`, `*.qlgenerator`, `*.mdimporter` |
| `resource-bundle`    | `Resources/*.bundle`, such as SwiftPM resource bundles          |
| `bundle`             | Any other `*.bundle`                                            |
| `login-item`         | `Contents/Library/LoginItems/*.app`                             |
| `helper-application` | `Contents/Helpers/*.app`                                        |
| `nested-application` | Any other nested `*.app`                                        |

The components also list:

- `privileged_helpers`: files directly in `Contents/Library/LaunchServices/`,
  where SMJobBless helpers live;
- `launchd_plists`: `.plist` files directly in `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents/`
  (`domain: "agent"`) or `Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/` (`domain: "daemon"`),
  as used by SMAppService;
- `helpers`: files directly in `Contents/Helpers/`.

Symlinks are reported by path in `symlinks`. Their targets are not inventoried,
so a versioned framework is described through its real `Versions/<version>/`
directories rather than `Versions/Current`. A framework's `info_plist_path` is
`null`, with a limitation explaining why, when it has more than one real
`Versions/<version>/` directory (even if only one of them holds a plist,
because `Versions/Current` decides which one applies) or when its single
version directory has no `Resources/Info.plist`.

AppleDouble sidecar files (`._*` and `__MACOSX/`) are inventory facts, but they
describe neighbouring files. They are excluded from roots, bundle roles, and the
anatomy components.

The projection does not read plists. Use `inspect_plist` on a bundle's
`info_plist_path` or a launchd plist to read `CFBundleExecutable`, identifiers,
`SMPrivilegedExecutables`, `BundleProgram`, URL schemes, and usage descriptions.
MCP calls require an existing `open_binary` or `open_bundle_resources` session,
including when `inspect_plist.path` is explicit. For a bundle without a resolved
executable, open its resource session first. The CLI `rea inspect-plist <path>`
opens the selected artifact for its one invocation.
Use `inspect_signature` on an executable candidate for code-signing claims.

## Dylib load resolution

`trace_dylib_resolution` answers which file each Mach-O dylib load reaches. It
runs on the active Mach-O, or on every executable in the active `.app`. Each
executable in a bundle (the main app, XPC services, app extensions, login items,
privileged helpers, and helper tools) is a separate process root with its own
`@executable_path`.

```sh
rea trace-dylib-resolution MyApp.app --json
rea trace-dylib-resolution MyApp.app --root Contents/MacOS/MyApp --architecture arm64 --json
```

```json
{
  "name": "trace_dylib_resolution",
  "arguments": { "roots": ["Contents/MacOS/MyApp"], "architecture": "arm64" }
}
```

Load commands are parsed in TypeScript from Mach-O and FAT headers, including
the `dylib_use_command` encoding newer linkers emit for flags such as delayed
initialization, and `LC_LAZY_LOAD_DYLIB_INFO` (`0x3a`). That command stores its
install name in a linkedit payload rather than in the load command itself.
Its flag and chain-start image offsets must lie in the slice VM range, which
is dyld's one-page floor extended by every segment except `__LINKEDIT`,
measured from the `__TEXT` vmaddr. Payload strings must start after the 24-byte
header. The load-path NUL must occur before the payload's final byte, matching
dyld's scan. Distinct payload bytes and payload-range lookups stay within the 16 MiB
limit, and a file range already read is reused. String scanning and UTF-8
checks count every reference, including repeats and overlaps, and stop at that
same aggregate. A slice retains at most 1024 of these commands; further copies are
unsupported instead of becoming one traced edge each. Symbol references,
including repeats, stop at 65536 per slice. A larger table is unsupported
instead of caching one string per offset.
Nothing is executed and no Apple tool is required, so the tool also works off
macOS.

Resolution follows dyld:

- `@executable_path` is the directory of the process root's executable. It is
  undetermined when the root is a library.
- `@loader_path` is the directory of the image that holds the load command, or
  of the image that owns the `LC_RPATH` entry being expanded.
- `@rpath` tries each `LC_RPATH` of the loading image first, then those of the
  image that loaded it, up to the process root.
- Dependencies load dependents-first in load-command order, and each image
  loads once per process. A later @rpath request whose install name matches an
  already loaded image reuses it.
- Symlinks such as `Versions/Current` are followed inside the analyzed root.
  An escape through `..` or an absolute link is `escapes-target`.
- Dyld path components are POSIX names. On Windows hosts, link text uses `\`
  as its separator, and a dyld component that contains `\` or `:` cannot name
  a file in the analyzed root, so its candidate is `absent`.

Each edge lists every candidate path tried, with its outcome: `resolved`,
`absent`, `not-mach-o`, `malformed`, `unsupported` (recognized Mach-O outside
parser coverage, such as big-endian images), `architecture-missing`,
`not-loadable`, `platform-mismatch`, `outside-target`, `escapes-target`, or
`undetermined`. `not-loadable` means a
matching-architecture Mach-O image was found but it is not a dylib and cannot
satisfy a dylib dependency. `platform-mismatch` means a matching-architecture
dylib was found but its observed platform is incompatible with the process.
These outcomes reject that candidate; dyld search may continue and resolve a
later candidate. Candidate outcomes describe individual search paths, while
`resolution.status` describes the final edge. For each selected process-root
slice, candidate slices are matched by CPU type and dyld's subtype preference
order, independently of FAT table order. An ARMv7s root slice prefers ARMv7s,
then ARMv7; other known ARM32 subtypes use their compatibility rows from
[Apple's dyld source](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/dyld/blob/dyld-852.2/src/dyld2.cpp#L2811-L3105).
An `x86_64h` process also loads generic `x86_64`. Unknown ARM32 subtype policy
remains undetermined when ARM32 candidate slices exist. This is a static model
keyed to the selected root slice; it does not observe the target device's host
CPU or prove which slice the device will execute. The edge's `resolution` is
one of:

| Status         | Meaning                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resolved`     | An image inside the analyzed root loads, and no earlier candidate was undeterminable.                                                                          |
| `conditional`  | An in-root image may load, but an earlier outside candidate, unmodeled environment input, or unknown platform compatibility can change which image dyld loads. |
| `unresolved`   | Every candidate is definitively absent or unusable inside the root.                                                                                            |
| `undetermined` | No candidate resolves inside the root, and some candidate lies outside it or depends on the environment.                                                       |

A `conditional` image is still traced, because it is an in-root candidate
that may load. Every edge below it has `loader_conditional: true`, and a
request that reuses it by install name is `conditional` too. An in-root dylib
with no platform load command remains unknown unless the root is an executable
with observed macOS platform and the candidate's CPU type is x86_64, i386, or arm64. In that macOS context,
[Apple's dyld](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/dyld/blob/fd8d0c4d52320ebf64db34f3cb280310d905c5ae/mach_o/UnsafeHeader.cpp#L1137-L1145) supplies an implicit macOS platform to legacy dylibs on those CPU
types. The candidate records `platform_basis: "macos-dyld-implicit"`; the
reported slice fields `platform: null` and `platforms: []` remain the parsed
facts. For other process contexts the platform remains unknown, coverage is
partial, and the candidate is not treated as incompatible. If a later known
candidate resolves, it remains the traced image with conditional resolution;
the trace does not claim the unknown candidate's dependency graph. Findings on
conditional edges say that they apply only if the conditional image loads.

Absolute install names that name a path beneath the analyzed root are checked
within that root, with symlinks and `..` resolved by the same bounded tree
resolver. Absolute paths outside the root, such as
`/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib`, are `outside-target`; on macOS 11 and later most
system libraries live in the dyld shared cache rather than on disk, so REA does
not check them against the host. Mach-O path strings are not converted from
`file:` URLs or looked up through unrelated host paths.

`findings` are derived, not observed:

- `required-load-unresolved`, `weak-load-unresolved`, and `lazy-load-unresolved`.
  `LC_LAZY_LOAD_DYLIB` and `LC_LAZY_LOAD_DYLIB_INFO` dependencies are resolved
  but not traversed, because dyld loads them on first use; an unresolved one is
  not a launch failure. `LC_LAZY_LOAD_DYLIB_INFO` has no compatibility version,
  so those fields are null. Its may-be-missing flag is reported as `weak`, and
  an unresolved dependency with that flag is not a first-use failure: dyld
  continues if the image is absent.
- `earlier-rpath-candidate-absent`: a compatible Mach-O placed at an earlier
  modeled search path could take precedence, subject to unmodeled search inputs
  and code-signing library validation. These findings do not establish which
  image dyld will load; use `inspect_signature` for signing metadata.
- `dyld-environment-present`: preserves observed `LC_DYLD_ENVIRONMENT` entries.
  Only an executable root supplies process settings; entries on library and
  other non-executable roots do not alter resolution or coverage. Applicable
  executable image-selection overrides are not modeled.

Empty dyld settings have different consumers. Modern dyld appends a slash and
image name to ordinary and fallback directory entries, so an empty entry can
search `/child.dylib` or `/Foo.framework/Foo`. REA retains uncertainty for those
unchecked paths; an empty fallback does not preempt an ordinary-search hit.
Empty versioned-directory lists do not scan a directory, and empty suffixes
only repeat the original candidate, so they do not add search uncertainty.
Reported command values are retained in all cases.

`verify:macos-bundle` checks the parser against `otool -l` for every traced
image. It also compares the predicted load order of two process roots with the
images dyld actually loads (`DYLD_PRINT_LIBRARIES`).

rea-docs-apple-ips.m:
# Apple IPS crash reports

`inspect_apple_ips` / `inspect-apple-ips` answers whether one selected local
Apple `.ips` file is a crash report (`bug_type` string `"309"`), which process,
exception, and termination facts that report records, which threads and
`usedImages` rows it lists, and which documented crash classes its strings
match. It reads the file without executing a target and does not require Xcode,
atos, a disassembler, or pwntools.

```bash
rea inspect-apple-ips /absolute/path/to/report.ips --json
```

The CLI resolves relative paths against the caller's working directory. MCP
requires an absolute filesystem path and preserves that exact selection:

```json
{
  "name": "inspect_apple_ips",
  "arguments": { "path": "/artifacts/report.ips" }
}
```

## Observations

The inline Evidence result contains the artifact path, SHA-256, and byte length.
`metadata` is the first-line JSON object. `bug_type` stays a string. The crash
body is parsed only when that string is `"309"`. Other types, including `"288"`
stackshots, return no crash result.

`process`, `exception`, `termination`, `faulting_thread`, `threads`, and
`images` reproduce documented body fields when present, including each image's
`name` and each frame's `symbolLocation` (as `symbol_location`, the byte offset
from the start of `recorded_symbol`). `termination` keeps the terminating
process as `by_proc` and `by_pid` and its `flags`; `process.parent_pid` keeps
`parentPid` next to `parent`; and `metadata` keeps `build_version` and
`platform`. Integers keep their
decimal literals and a hexadecimal form, including arm64e registers above
2^53. Frame roles follow the recorded frame index: row zero of the resolved
faulting thread is `faulting_instruction`, row zero of other threads is
`current_instruction`, and later rows are `return_address`. Each runtime
address uses that row's own image base and offset. The recorded `inline` flag
does not supply a missing offset or authorize borrowing another row's address.
When `faultingThread` is missing or does not resolve to a recorded thread
object, row-zero roles are `unknown`; the recorded lookup remains available.
A translated process records Rosetta's registers in a nested
`threadState.rosetta` object; each one is reported as `rosetta.<name>` and
counts toward the register budget. A [public ReportCrash `.ips` log](https://github.com/Mortennn/Dozer/issues/189)
shows `rosetta.tmp2`, `tmp1`, and `tmp0` beside ordinary x86 registers. The
test fixture quotes that register excerpt inside an authored report body; it
does not generate a new Rosetta crash during the test.
Observed JSON strings retain `""`; `null` means the field was missing or JSON
`null`. This includes image paths, frame symbols, process text, and the older
string `osVersion` form. Unlisted JSON keys and generic register names also
retain empty spellings. An empty image architecture remains recorded as `""`
while `uuid_unknown` stays true, since that spelling does not establish an
architecture. An empty UUID is malformed, so its exact spelling appears in
`coverage.type_mismatches` and its canonical UUID remains unknown.
`process.os_version` keeps the producer's dictionary (`train`, `build`,
`release_type`, `is_embedded`) or the older string form. Image UUIDs are uppercase 8-4-4-4-12; an all-zero UUID
or a missing or empty `arch` is `uuid_unknown`. Image `source` letters keep their
documented meaning (`P` process, `S` shared cache, `C` shared cache library,
`K` kernel, `U` kernel cache, `T` kernel text exec, `A` absolute). Keys the
documentation does not list remain in `unlisted_keys` or `unlisted_body_keys`.

Each frame's `image_index` refers to its entry in `images`. Image architecture,
UUID and `uuid_unknown` are retained once on that image. Resolve the reference
when using those facts; an absent or out-of-range index leaves the image
unknown. This avoids repeating image text for every stack frame.

A present value whose JSON type differs from the documented one is never read
as absent: it is listed in `coverage.type_mismatches` with its path, the
expected type, and the observed type, and `coverage.status` becomes
`partial`. A crash body without `threads` or `usedImages` is also `partial`.
Malformed image UUID strings likewise make coverage partial; their exact spelling
is retained in the mismatch's `recorded_value`, while the canonical image UUID
remains unknown. Both 32 hexadecimal digits and canonical hyphenated UUIDs are accepted.
Unresolved thread/image references also make coverage partial. A rejected
integer lookup keeps its exact decimal literal in `recorded_integer`, including
negative values and values above uint32. Valid uint32 lookup values remain in
`faulting_thread` or `image_index` even when the referenced row is unavailable.

`classification` matches only documented SIGKILL codes (compared by their
canonical hexadecimal form), `EXC_GUARD` subtypes,
pointer-authentication suffixes, and dyld missing-library strings. A report
that matches none of those rules is `unclassified`.

Opened Mach-O and dSYM UUID joins remain unobserved. Symbol names printed
inside the report are recorded claims and are not verified. Linux ELF cores
use the separate [recorded crash](recorded-crashes.md) workflow.

## Limits and failures

The selected file is limited to 1 MiB by default (16 MiB maximum). At most 256
threads, 8192 frames, 1024 `usedImages` rows, and 16384 `threadState`
register slots are examined by default (4096 / 65536 / 4096 / 262144
maximum). Budgets are checked before each row is parsed, and body members the
report does not interpret are syntax-checked without being kept. Fixed
allowances bound JSON nesting (64 levels), unlisted key names per object
(1024), and `termination.reasons` entries (256). Malformed metadata, a
truncated crash body, invalid UTF-8, a NUL in the text, and exhausted budgets
fail without partial success.

`max_integer_text_bytes` (`--max-integer-text-bytes` in the CLI) separately
bounds retained decimal and hexadecimal integer text, including every derived
runtime address and rejected lookup literal. Its default is 8 MiB of UTF-16 text storage and its maximum is
64 MiB. Each appearance counts, even when an object could be shared in memory
but would be serialized more than once. The parser reserves a conservative
upper bound before numeric conversion or address expansion, then releases the
unused reservation after each value. It reuses the parsed source integer when
the same image base contributes to many frames.

Raise this per-call allowance on the next call when more room is needed; no
restart is required. File-size and row budgets do not raise it. This allowance
is separate from JSON wire size, MCP response limits and the client's receive
buffer. An exhausted allowance reports a typed resource error without partial
success or truncated integer facts.

```bash
rea inspect-apple-ips /absolute/path/to/report.ips --max-integer-text-bytes 16777216 --json
```

This workflow does not execute a target, launch atos, or search for dSYMs.

rea-docs-desktop-applications.m:
# Desktop installation directories

Use `inspect_desktop_application` when an installation directory is the target
and its runtime is unknown. It reads directory entries, selected headers and
bounded metadata, then reports runtime candidates, supporting files, component
path markers and concrete follow-up operations. No native provider or active
binary session is needed. It does not run the application, extract archives,
follow child symlinks, contact services or change target files.

## MCP

```json
{ "path": "/artifacts/MyApplication" }
```

Default `detail: "summary"` retains complete source Evidence in the session and
returns candidates with representative supporting paths, counts, coverage,
limitations and grouped next probes. `normalized_result.parent_evidence_id`
identifies the complete record. A server without Evidence retention refuses
summary delivery before reading the target; select `detail: "complete"` to
receive every retained fact inline.

Read exact files in one request:

```json
{
  "source": {
    "kind": "retained-evidence",
    "evidence_id": "ev_<parent-sha256>"
  },
  "view": {
    "kind": "desktop-application",
    "collection": "files",
    "paths": ["Game_Data/Managed/Assembly-CSharp.dll", "GameAssembly.dll"],
    "fields": ["path", "read_status", "ranges", "facts", "issues"],
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 16
  }
}
```

Collections are `files`, `omissions`, `candidates`, `components` and `next_probes`.
Files and omissions accept exact `paths` and batched `file_ids` / `omission_ids`.
Files also accept `has_issues: true` to select probe diagnostics directly, or
`false` to select rows without reported issues. This filter uses the retained
issue facts; it does not re-read targets or infer that uninspected files are healthy.
When both are supplied, all filters apply; an empty selection returns no rows.
Omission records retain the observed path, kind and stable `omission_id`; their
payloads are not read, and other special-entry metadata remains unavailable.
`candidates` accepts exact `families`.
Omitted selectors match all retained rows; an empty selector matches none.
Every collection supports `fields`, `offset` and `limit`; its stable row ID is
always included. Selection changes delivery, not source inspection. Pages keep
source coverage and parent Evidence links. Page exhaustion does not establish
absence in a partial source. Complete Evidence remains accessible through
`get_evidence` and Evidence bundle export.

The summary's `probe_issues` counts files with reported issues and their retained
issue entries. It previews at most two such files, including stable `file_id`,
read status and the first issue. Path/reason previews use at most 256 UTF-16 units
each without splitting surrogate pairs; `text_truncated` marks shortened text,
and `preview_truncated` marks additional files. These are display prefixes;
full caller paths and all reasons remain in Evidence. Counts describe retained
observations, while source coverage still identifies partial inspection.

Use `inspect_analysis_view` with `collection: "files", has_issues: true` and
`fields: ["path", "read_status", "issues"]` for exact reasons, with the usual
paging and parent links. It intersects with exact paths and batched file IDs.

An ASAR inventory probe first selects its exact path with `open_binary`; then
call `inspect_artifact` on that active target. Directory inspection itself does
not select or replace the session target. The JavaScript application workflow
accepts its own selected path directly.

## CLI

The one-shot CLI returns complete Evidence by default. For compact output,
explicitly retain it in a bundle:

```bash
rea inspect-desktop-application /artifacts/MyApplication \
  --detail summary --evidence_output /reports/application.evidence.json --json
```

This returns `summary` Evidence and an `evidence_bundle` publication receipt.
Existing output files are never overwritten. Summary delivery requires
`--evidence_output`, checked before analysis. `inspect-evidence-bundle` selects
saved records; an exact saved record can also feed `inspect-analysis-view`.
`--detail complete` returns source Evidence inline and can optionally write the
same bundle. Export writes only the caller-selected output file.

## Facts and uncertainty

| Family       | Evidence used                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| .NET         | A PE optional header declares a nonempty CLI directory.                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Unity Mono   | A managed assembly below `*_Data/Managed` or `Contents/Resources/Data/Managed` has an exact UnityEngine assembly reference.                                                                                                                    |
| Unity IL2CPP | A recognized IL2CPP metadata magic (with the raw version when complete) coexists with a conventionally named native `GameAssembly.dll`, `GameAssembly.so`, `GameAssembly.dylib` or `libil2cpp.so` image. Build correspondence remains unknown. |
| Godot        | A `GDPC` header at file start or a validated executable trailer offset.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| GameMaker    | A bounded `FORM` container starts with a `GEN8` chunk. The scan probes conventional `data.win`, `game.unx`, and `game.ios` data files for that header.                                                                                         |
| Unreal       | `Content/Paks` path conventions or an IoStore TOC signature; arbitrary `.pak` filenames are insufficient.                                                                                                                                      |
| Electron     | A `resources/app.asar` or `resources/default_app.asar` path convention; archive validity is unverified.                                                                                                                                        |

When the four-byte metadata magic is present but version bytes are incomplete,
the fact retains `raw_version: null`; it does not offer an IL2CPP metadata
inspection probe. A complete magic/version prefix with supported raw version
24, 27, 29, 31 or 39 offers an `inspect_il2cpp_metadata` follow-up at its
admitted file path, including when no native library was found. This probe does
not establish full metadata validity or correspondence to a native binary;
version 24 inspection still applies only to supported header layouts. See
[IL2CPP metadata](il2cpp-metadata.md).

Candidates are derived or inferred from these facts and do not prove loading or
execution. BepInEx, MelonLoader, Easy Anti-Cheat and BattlEye labels identify
path conventions only; runtime presence stays unknown. No bypass is provided.

`file_id` includes the admitted root namespace, recorded path and available filesystem identity. The caller-selected root path and admitted canonical path/root identity are both retained; `local_path` identifies each observed file for follow-up operations. The selected root may be a symlink; child symlinks are not followed. Exact
metadata integers remain decimal strings. Read ranges have offsets, byte counts
and SHA-256 digests; typed facts expose CLI RVAs, metadata/pack versions and
assembly tokens. Directory and symlink identities unavailable from traversal
remain null.

The directory's `snapshot_sha256` commits to retained paths, omission kinds,
available metadata and range digests, composed through the admitted root,
entry and omission identities. Caller ceilings, coverage counters, diagnostic
wording and interpretation facts remain in Evidence, outside source identity.
The same observations under different generous limits share a snapshot digest;
Evidence IDs still preserve request parameters and reported coverage. Different
retained entries or read ranges change the source snapshot.
Omission records share the entry and representation budgets and can be fetched
independently through their view.
**It is not a digest of all file contents.** These are sequential stable entry
observations, not an atomic directory snapshot. Unread bytes remain unknown.

## Resource bounds and reuse

Defaults are 20,000 examined entries and 8 MiB of total probe reads. Callers may
select up to 100,000 entries and 64 MiB. A separate 32 MiB conservative
representation budget bounds retained paths and facts before growth. Limits
and failed probes produce partial coverage. Traversal and reads are serial.
Each reader admits one inspection at a time; overlapping requests receive a
retryable capacity refusal without cancelling the admitted caller.

Unity reference decoding stops after a witness in each `Data/Managed` directory;
other assemblies' references remain unexamined, while their headers are still
checked. AssemblyRef facts decode names and tokens only; they do not decode or
hash unrelated key/culture/hash payloads or establish runtime binding. Pack contents, encrypted data, metadata/address correspondence and
section-embedded PCKs without a trailer are separate capabilities.

Filesystem results are not cached across calls. Retained views reuse validated
immutable metadata without rescanning files or retaining another inventory.

rea-docs-electron-observation.m:
# Electron file-page observation

REA can attach to an Electron/Chromium CDP endpoint and inspect existing `file://` renderer pages without evaluating JavaScript or invoking Electron APIs. The request supplies the endpoint directly; REA accepts only literal-port loopback HTTP endpoints. Selecting an endpoint exposes every Electron target it serves, including local file paths and page metadata.

Disconnecting the inspection's page session can clear caller-owned
`navigator.platform` emulation inside Chromium. REA cannot restore another
client's complete user-agent/client-hint configuration. Use a disposable target
or let the owning client reapply its configuration; see the shared
[CDP state limitation](browser-observation.md#provider-authorities).

This passive runtime surface is distinct from the target-free static
[`analyze_javascript_application`](javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md)
workflow. Static analysis reads a local ASAR or extracted directory without
executing application code. Passive observation inspects an existing Electron
page. The results keep static inferences and runtime observations distinct.
Packaged fuse state is a separate static read:
[`inspect_electron_fuses`](electron-fuses.md) reports whether this binary will
honor Inspector flags, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`, embedded ASAR integrity, and
`app.asar`-only loading.
Use the separate
[`reconcile_javascript_runtime`](javascript-runtime-reconciliation.md) workflow
when both Evidence sets already exist.

## Target boundary

The request supplies a literal-port loopback endpoint and, for inspection, a
target ID. REA accepts local hostless `file://` URLs that resolve to regular
files, including pages a packaged application serves from inside `app.asar`.
For those, the first `.asar` path component that is a regular file is the
archive, the remainder must name a regular file in its header, and the reported
path is the canonical archive path joined with that member. Remote hosts,
encoded separators in the pathname, ASAR directories or links, and nonexistent paths are
rejected. The endpoint exposes every eligible target and its local path
metadata. Query strings and fragments do not participate in filesystem path
admission, including their encoded separator text. Listing and inspection
Evidence both retain the observed browser product/revision; host platform and
architecture remain explicitly unknown.

Cancellation stops further file authorization after an already-started filesystem
operation settles. ASAR descriptor-close failures remain typed incomplete cleanup
with an exact retryable owner; they are not treated as a missing or unauthorized
page. A later authorization and provider shutdown retry retained descriptors
before reporting their release. Failed listing retains its already-authorized
target prefix and explicit remaining-target uncertainty through cleanup errors
and exact-owner retries.

## Workflow

`list_electron_targets` returns every eligible target served by the supplied endpoint in one inline array.

For the MCP follow-up call, pass the same literal-loopback endpoint and the selected target ID to `inspect_electron_page`. REA rediscovers targets and validates the ID against the live endpoint before inspection.

```bash
rea list-electron-targets http://127.0.0.1:9223 --json
rea inspect-electron-page http://127.0.0.1:9223 TARGET_ID \
  --observation-ms 100 --json
```

Script content is excluded by default. Setting `include_script_sources` in the
request returns the selected target's script sources:

```bash
rea inspect-electron-page http://127.0.0.1:9223 TARGET_ID \
  --include-script-sources \
  --json
```

The normalized result contains canonical local paths, frame and DOM
structure, resource metadata, stable script/resource identities, explicit
completeness, and content-addressed script artifacts. Resource sizes are unknown
when omitted or invalid; supplied invalid sizes also produce an explicit
completeness diagnostic.

DOM node indices retain their snapshot positions. Invalid rows are omitted with
completeness diagnostics, so `total_nodes` can exceed the retained node count
and a parent index can refer to an omitted source node.

Script metadata retains its execution-context frame ID when CDP supplies one and
records admission separately in `frame_scope`. An `authorized` scope refers to
the observed document generation; `unknown` retains the known frame ID without
claiming authorization and makes script coverage attach-limited. Historical
captures may omit this field, which leaves that admission fact unknown.
Scripts from document generations whose frames were explicitly excluded by
local-file policy are omitted before script-source reads. Frame identity can
come from the script event's own auxiliary data or its observed execution
context; contradictory identities are not aligned.
`frame_claims.script_event_frame_id` and
`frame_claims.execution_context_frame_id` preserve the actual observed claims
from those two sources. Both remain available when their disagreement leaves
the resolved `frame_id` null and `frame_scope` unknown. An omitted claim is
unobserved, not proof that a frame was absent.
Frames describe the current inventory; script observations can retain earlier
authorized frames that have since detached.

`has_source_url` preserves CDP's sourceURL declaration flag as true, false, or
unknown (`null`, or omitted in historical captures). A script's canonical
`file_path` is the admitted local-file URL or supplied sourceURL label. It does
not verify that the runtime bytes came from that disk file; captured source
bytes have their own digest. `reported_url` retains the original URL or label
before canonical path admission. Labels remain distinct from filesystem provenance.
The capture also
inventories worker, service-worker, and shared-worker targets with
validated opener-target and parent-frame IDs. Worker discovery uses passive
target metadata; REA does not attach to or execute code in those targets.
Script metadata uses the shared 8 MiB JSON-byte allowance for each retained
representation: incoming drafts and normalized capture metadata. Admission
counts escaped strings, frame claims, and provenance fields before retaining
them or serializing metadata for a digest. Exhaustion preserves earlier records
and reports counted `resource_budget_exhausted` script omissions; a later
smaller record may still fit. This allowance adds no script-count cap and is
separate from script-source bytes.
Script-source collection retains at most 32 MiB of UTF-8 text across scripts
and shares a 20-second collection deadline. Omitted sources retain their script
metadata and an explicit reason; later smaller sources may still fit after an
oversized source is omitted. The separate 64 MiB CDP response limit bounds one
wire message before retention admission, rather than total transient memory.
The source budget adds no script-count cap. Like every
target, frame, script, and resource, a worker URL must resolve to a local
file before it is retained. Relationship IDs improve
attribution but do not prove which static module started a worker or that its
work completed.
Missing opener and parent relationships leave worker ownership unknown. Such
targets are withheld with an `unattributed_target` exclusion and unavailable
`workers` coverage, even when their URL names a local file. Explicit foreign
relationships remain `out_of_target_scope`; malformed supplied relationship IDs
are `invalid_protocol_value`.

Inspection does not retain DOM values, execute renderer code, navigate, click,
invoke Electron IPC, close a target, or terminate the application.

## Active Electron scenarios

The scenario request supplies the Electron executable and application entry
point, plus any arguments and actions. The application root defaults to the
entry point's parent directory and can be supplied when the app uses a different
root. REA launches that executable through
the official Playwright Electron API and owns its lifetime. It accepts click/wait actions,
window-targeted renderer reload/crash actions, and synthetic `open-url` or
`second-instance` deep-link delivery. It records capture-scoped window and
WebContents identities, process metrics, and IPC channel and value-shape metadata.
Payload values are not retained.

`window_index` selects from Playwright's current Page list at the start of each action. REA resolves that Page to its corresponding BrowserWindow once; the action's `target` uses the BrowserWindow's capture-scoped `window_id`, matching the window inventory. Reordering either enumeration after selection does not retarget the action. Handle cleanup failures retain the completed action records and remain owned for provider cleanup retry.

Run the real fixture verifier with an operator-provided Electron runtime:

```bash
REA_ELECTRON_EXECUTABLE=/absolute/path/to/electron npm run verify:electron
```

This operation actively launches and interacts with the selected target. It is
not a passive CDP observation. The owned process keeps normal host filesystem
and network privileges, so lifecycle ownership does not make it a sandbox.

The CLI and MCP surfaces accept the same schema. For a JSON request file:

```bash
rea capture-electron-scenario scenario.json --json
```

The result records one status and target per declared action; actions after a
failed or cancelled action are not run and are recorded as `cancelled` with a
not-executed error. It also records correlated app/window/WebContents,
preload, session, navigation, shell, permission, popup, download, protocol,
native-addon, process, and IPC timeline events. IPC channels and argument-shape
metadata retain their observed lengths; payload values are never retained.
Renderer crash/restart and deep-link actions are synthetic
scenario controls; their attempted and observed outcomes remain in the
timeline. The active hook blocks and records the shell methods listed below
and selected navigation, permission, download, popup, updater, and
OS-integration APIs. These method patches do not contain direct filesystem,
network, native-addon, or other unpatched target effects. The timeline
is explicitly partial when attachment starts after application activity. The
startup, including the initial state snapshot, has a 60-second deadline.
Actions wait until completion or request cancellation; a click whose target
never appears, or a `wait` without `window_index` in an app that opens no
window, remains pending until cancelled. After cancellation, the final state
read has 5 seconds before REA keeps the initial snapshot instead; the
cancellation keeps the caller's reason and records that expiry in its
diagnostics.
The shell policy is owned by `blockedShellResults` in
`scripts/electron-active-hook-boundaries.cjs`. Its synchronous blocks are:
`showItemInFolder` returns `undefined` and `writeShortcutLink` returns `false`.
Their `shell-attempt` events record the blocked phase and argument shapes;
neither result means the requested host operation occurred. The existing
`openExternal`, `openPath`, and `trashItem` blocks reject their promises.
The `trashItem` block prevents that call from reaching the OS trash operation;
it does not intercept other ways the application can remove files.
CLI SIGINT/SIGTERM requests cancellation and awaits owned-process cleanup.
Window IDs, URLs, and cached titles come from one main-process Electron snapshot,
so a crashed renderer does not require a successful renderer-side title query.
Window instrumentation uses Electron's window-created event, including runtimes
with a read-only `BrowserWindow` export. Preload configuration comes from the
window's runtime metadata, including Electron's optional internal preload
descriptor when web preferences omit it. This descriptor is verified on
Electron 44.7.0; runtimes that expose neither representation retain an unavailable
path. A configured path or working IPC handler does not prove preload execution.
If cleanup cannot be verified, the error retains collected observations in
`details.partial_observation` and marks their application cleanup `unverified`.
Cleanup uncertainty does not authorize signaling unrelated processes.

On Linux, Chromium-based processes can overwrite the initial environment memory
exposed through `/proc/<pid>/environ`. The environment may be readable while
`REA_PROCESS_RUN_ID` is absent, even if the application still sees it through
`process.env`. REA reports the missing marker and leaves lineage ownership and
cleanup unverified; the PID, executable, or parent relationship cannot replace
that ownership proof. This limitation can affect owned Electron captures on
native Linux as well as WSL. It does not establish that all Electron versions or
Linux environments behave the same way.

Main-process IPC recording keeps original-function removal for `on` and `once`
registrations and records a fired `once` callback once. Native Node.js owns
`once` registration, firing and callable dispatch as well as removal order and
traversal, including listeners registered by removal observers;
the hook translates only its own recording wrappers at the removal boundary.
Wrapper metadata uses weak keys and does not retain removed registrations.
Wrapper metadata operations, private collection methods and traversal constructors are captured
before target startup; later replacement of their global bindings does not
change listener registration or removal.

Native runtimes differ in whether `once` consults callback `.call` or `.apply`.
The hook observes actual callback entry without imposing another runtime's
property reads or argument-list representation. Application methods selected by
native dispatch keep their original receiver and argument-list object; opaque
methods produce a `custom-call` or `custom-apply` observation gap when callback
execution cannot be established.

If native wrapper creation or registration-method lookup could expose private
instrumentation through an application getter, setter or Proxy, registration
stays native and unwrapped. The `once-metadata` observation gap identifies that
unobserved registration attempt; it does not prove registration or delivery. The original callback,
metadata writes and native method receivers are preserved, including when
registration fails. Later registrations resume normal observation. Non-callable
`call`/`apply` properties produce failed observation gaps when native dispatch reads
them; callback entry is not fabricated.

An `on` listener's application-defined `.apply` receives the original argument-list
object unchanged. Borrowing the exposed method preserves its dynamic receiver.
Because that method owns argument interpretation and may not
invoke the callback, the hook records a bounded `ipc-observation-gap` timeline
entry with the registered channel rather than an IPC invocation. Its empty
`argument_shapes` means unobserved arguments, not a zero-argument callback;
callback execution and result remain unknown. Coverage and retention include
these gaps even when their individual records are dropped. Normal native
dispatch continues to record actual invocation frames. Evidence snapshots copy
retained arrays and counters without invoking application iterators or Array
species.

Listener-chain recognition distinguishes owned, unowned and unknown metadata.
Data links may be inherited; absence is established only after completing the
bounded prototype lookup. Exhausting either walk, encountering a getter or seeing a Proxy leaves
ownership unknown. The hook preserves native registration without adding another
recording wrapper and retains a `listener-chain` observation gap after successful
registration. This gap does not prove IPC delivery. An existing inner recording
wrapper can still report its actual invocation; otherwise callback activity
remains unobserved. Setter-only properties have a known undefined read.
Data-descriptor parsing is shared with removal normalization.

This does not establish complete JavaScript function introspection equivalence.
Caller-defined `.listener` properties can change the identity exposed by
`listeners()` and meta-events; accessors and Proxy metadata are not followed for
wrapper recognition. Re-registering a raw recording wrapper on another channel
retains the original registration's channel attribution.
Mutating `.listener` on a raw recording wrapper can also prevent removal through
application decorators that bypass the hook's removal methods. When a removal
request reaches the hook's methods and its registration order is known, private
callback ownership preserves removal by the original function and the newest
matching registration when public metadata is changed or deleted. Native removal
still determines getter execution, exceptions and removal meta-events.

If registration or removal methods differ from the Node methods captured at hook
initialization, the hook leaves listener callbacks unwrapped and records a
`listener-registration` observation gap. The application keeps its original
callback and receiver; callback execution remains unobserved. This comparison
assumes Node's EventEmitter prototype has not itself been globally decorated
before hook initialization. The provider loads the hook before the application
and excludes `NODE_OPTIONS` from the child environment. It preserves selected
`DISPLAY`, `XAUTHORITY` and `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` values, including the caller-selected
X11 authorization-file path.

An opaque later listener or unsupported emitter state can prevent proof of
removal order. The hook then delegates removal
to the native method and records a `listener-removal` gap rather than claiming
which registration was removed. These gaps are distinct from dropped records
and do not establish IPC delivery or successful removal.

### Target fuse prerequisites

Active scenario capture requires that the target Electron executable honors Node CLI inspector flags (`--inspect` or `--remote-debugging-port`) so that Playwright can establish its DevTools protocol session.

When an Electron executable explicitly disables the `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` fuse (or removes the capability), `capture-electron-scenario` fails immediately before process launch with an `AnalysisUnsupportedTargetError` ("unsupported_target") rather than waiting for the startup deadline. For targets with disabled inspector fuses, use passive CDP inspection via `inspect_electron_page` or run against an unrestricted development binary with the extracted `app.asar`.

The real verifier exercises compiled CLI and stdio MCP discovery, page/script
inspection, static/runtime reconciliation, active observation, and CLI SIGTERM
cleanup before checking the IPC, renderer crash/reload, utility/child-process,
deep-link, and blocked-effect fixture. A cleanup error keeps the full lane failed
even when the retained capture contains useful observations.

Active Electron Evidence can also be supplied to
[`reconcile_javascript_runtime`](javascript-runtime-reconciliation.md). That
projection is intentionally target-only and partial: it binds the selected
application path and capture outcome to the static graph, while frames, scripts,
workers, and execution claims remain unavailable until a separate passive runtime
capture provides them.

ASAR observation reads the header through one open file handle and validates its
declared lengths against the archive size. Header/index admission is the same
budget used by static ASAR reads: 16 MiB / 16777216 bytes by default, seeded by
`REA_ASAR_MAX_HEADER_BYTES` (at most 256 MiB). In MCP,
`update_analysis_settings` can override `asar.max_header_bytes` for new
operations without restarting REA. Cached headers are checked against each
operation's admission, including after a decrease. See the
[settings design](design/limits-and-recovery.md#failure-and-retry).
An oversized header is
not parsed; selecting a member path does not bypass admission, and the page
stays unauthorized. The header cache separately retains at most that many bytes
of already-admitted encoded headers across eight archives. Evicting that cache does not raise admission.

# Electron fuse state

`inspect_electron_fuses` / `inspect-electron-fuses` answers whether a packaged
Electron app will honor `--inspect` and `--inspect-brk`, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`,
embedded ASAR integrity validation, and loading application code only from
`app.asar`. It reads the fuse wire stored in the Electron binary. It does not
launch the app, modify fuse bytes, or use the network.

```bash
rea inspect-electron-fuses /Applications/Example.app --json
```

The CLI resolves a relative path against the caller's working directory. MCP
requires an absolute filesystem path and preserves that exact selection:

```json
{
  "name": "inspect_electron_fuses",
  "arguments": { "path": "/Applications/Example.app" }
}
```

On POSIX hosts, the CLI preserves path components so symlinks are followed
before parent (`..`) steps. Bundle selections may end in `.` or parent steps
through real directories; a terminal parent step through a directory symlink
is rejected. Windows CLI paths retain native drive and separator resolution.

Check this before `observe_javascript_runtime` with `electron-main`. When
`EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` is disabled or removed, Electron ignores
Inspector flags, and a later target listing can simply show no main-process
target.

## What is read

On macOS, pass the `.app` bundle or the Electron Framework binary. Bundle and
framework selection first tries the top-level `Electron Framework` binary,
then `Versions/Current/Electron Framework`, then
`Versions/A/Electron Framework`. Symlinks are followed only while they stay
inside that framework.
On Windows and Linux, pass the main Electron executable. The wire lives in
that executable rather than in `app.asar`.

The inline Evidence result contains:

- the selected path, the resolved regular file, its SHA-256, size, and container
  format (`mach-o`, `mach-o-universal`, `pe`, or `elf`);
- one slice entry for a thin Mach-O, PE, or ELF file, and one entry per slice of
  a universal Mach-O, with file-absolute `sentinel_offset` values;
- `wire_version`, `declared_length`, and ordered fuses `{ index, name, state, raw_byte }`;
- `sentinel_count`, including zero and more than one;
- `runtime_implications`, each marked `relationship: "derivation"` and tied to
  the fuse index it came from.

Version 1 names, in index order, are `RunAsNode`, `EnableCookieEncryption`,
`EnableNodeOptionsEnvironmentVariable`, `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments`,
`EnableEmbeddedAsarIntegrityValidation`, `OnlyLoadAppFromAsar`,
`LoadBrowserProcessSpecificV8Snapshot`, `GrantFileProtocolExtraPrivileges`,
and `WasmTrapHandlers`. An index past that table, or any index on another wire
version, keeps `name: null` and the raw byte.

Wire bytes are `0x30` disabled, `0x31` enabled, and `0x72` removed. Any other
byte is `unknown`. A removed fuse is not enabled: Inspector flags and
`ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` are not honored, and application code is not restricted
to `app.asar`. On macOS and Windows, a removed or disabled
`EnableEmbeddedAsarIntegrityValidation` byte means embedded ASAR integrity is
not enforced, and an enabled byte means it is enforced. Electron compiles that
validation only on macOS and Windows. On a Linux ELF executable the observed
byte is preserved and the enforcement outcome is `unknown`.

## Unknown and multiple sentinels

No sentinel means the fuse state is unknown. It does not mean the fuses are
disabled. A wire that continues past the slice is reported as truncated, with
only the fuse bytes that were present. Two or more sentinels in one slice are
all reported. REA does not pick one.

Fuse bytes do not prove that the application enables Inspector some other way,
for example through `app.commandLine` or a remote-debugging switch in
application code.

The selected file must be a regular file, or a bundle that resolves to one.
Symlinks are followed only inside `Electron Framework.framework`. The reader
admits at most 1 GiB, searches with 256 KiB windows, and keeps at most 32
sentinels per slice. A real nine-fuse, one-slice result is about 1,200 CLI
tokens; a two-slice result is about 1,300 tokens. Exact size varies with path
lengths and limitations. This inspection creates no temporary files and does
not modify the selected bytes.

# Flattened devicetree inspection

`inspect_devicetree` / `rea inspect-devicetree` reads a local DTB without an
engine, target execution or external tools. It supports FDT versions 16 and 17;
other versions return `unsupported_target`. Corrupt recognized blobs return
`invalid_request`, and exhausted budgets return `resource_constraint` without
partial success.

```bash
rea inspect-devicetree /artifacts/board.dtb --json
rea inspect-devicetree /artifacts/board.dtb --detail summary --evidence_output /artifacts/board-evidence.json --json
```

The complete Evidence includes the artifact SHA-256, validated header fields,
64-bit memory reservations as exact hexadecimal strings, and a flat node tree
with explicit parent paths. Each property retains its file offset, byte length,
and up to 256 raw bytes as hex. `truncated` qualifies the preview only; parsing
coverage includes the entire declared tree. Version 16 has no declared structure
size, so `header.size_dt_struct` is null.

Derived fields carry `confidence: derived`: standard ASCII string lists, scalar
phandles and cell counts, and `reg` tuples using the parent's `#address-cells`
and `#size-cells` (defaults 2 and 1). Zero-cell components are null (omitted), distinct from an encoded zero. Cell
counts above four, invalid counts and incomplete tuples remain undecoded with a
limitation. Addresses are bus-local; no `ranges` translation is attempted.
Invalid or ambiguous strings remain raw, rather than being guessed.

The summary is labeled derived and includes root compatible/model, chosen
bootargs/stdout-path and aliases. An undecodable alias retains its name with a
null path; it is not silently treated as absent. Single-cell `interrupt-parent`, `remote-endpoint` and `msi-parent`
references resolve through phandle declarations. Missing or duplicate targets
have null target paths. A node whose `phandle` and `linux,phandle` disagree
adds a limitation, and references to either value stay unresolved. A present
`phandle` that is not one cell also adds a limitation; `linux,phandle` cannot
resolve that node when the canonical declaration is malformed. Binding-specific
reference arrays and overlays are not resolved; an empty reference list does not
prove absence of hardware links.

MCP `detail: summary` retains complete Evidence in the session. Follow its
`parent_evidence_id` with `inspect_analysis_view`:

```json
{
  "source": { "kind": "retained-evidence", "evidence_id": "ev:<digest>" },
  "view": {
    "kind": "devicetree",
    "collection": "properties",
    "path": "/serial@1000",
    "offset": 0,
    "limit": 32
  }
}
```

Collections are `nodes` (identity and property counts), `properties` (requires an
exact node path), `reservations`, and `references`. Pages use retained parsed
facts and do not reopen the file. Each page carries fixed-size context
(artifact, header, coverage and counts) rather than the summary strings, so a
large `bootargs` value does not repeat on every page. Source indices are scoped to the selected
collection and parent Evidence; property indices are scoped to their node.

| Input budget     | Default | Ceiling |
| ---------------- | ------: | ------: |
| `max_file_bytes` |   4 MiB |  16 MiB |
| `max_nodes`      |   8,192 |  65,536 |
| `max_properties` |  32,768 | 262,144 |
| `max_depth`      |      64 |     256 |

Decoded names, paths, values and row overhead share a fixed 32 MiB representation
allowance, charged before expansion. It has no runtime override.

The reservation count also uses `max_properties`. CLI flags use kebab case,
for example `--max-nodes 16384`. View pages contain at most 256 rows.

## Verification

Synthetic tests cover v16/v17, malformed headers/blocks/names/tokens, resource
limits, derived values, and CLI/MCP delivery including retained pages after
removing the input. The optional real lane requires **dtc 1.8.1**:

```bash
npm run build:cached
node scripts/verify/firmware/devicetree.mjs
```

It compiles a DTS with reserved-memory, chosen, aliases and phandles, compares
REA's node paths against `dtc -I dtb -O dts`, and checks the derived report.
`REA_DTC_PATH` selects the verification executable; it is not runtime setup.

The dtc 1.8.1 lane ran on macOS arm64 with Node 26.5.0. Its seven node paths
matched the decompiled tree. The report included `model: "REA DTB verification"`,
`bootargs: "console=ttyS0"`, alias `serial0 -> /serial@1000`, reservation
`0x80000000 + 0x1000`, and a resolved reference from `/consumer` to
`/serial@1000`. The deliberately minimal remote-endpoint fixture produces dtc
graph-binding warnings; this lane verifies FDT structure and selected property
derivations, not hardware-binding validity.

A repeat run of that complete compile/decompile/CLI verification took 2.13 s
elapsed, 1.52 s user CPU and 0.27 s system CPU under `/usr/bin/time -l`. This is a
small fixture with warm filesystem caches, not a cold-start or large-board
benchmark. Peak process-family memory and whole-workflow token usage were not
measured; the sandbox denied the memory-reporting system query. No pre-feature
equivalent REA workflow exists for comparison. The pinned Node 24.22.1/npm
11.16.0 toolchain was unavailable; dependency installation used the local cache
with Node 26.5.0/npm 12.2.0 instead.

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/installation.md) for provider configuration and manual MCP registration. MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full` in your MCP registration when you need the complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. Which agents can use REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the [supported agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use [manual MCP registration](docs/installation.md#mcp-registry).
Do I need Hopper, Ghidra or IDA? Deep native analysis uses one of them. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra and IDA use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/installation.md#hopper).
Do I need to start Hopper first? REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See [Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).
What does installing the skill from skills.sh do? The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/installation.md#skill-only-installation).
What code does REA return? Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.
Does REA upload my app? REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` For agent setup through `npx`: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.

# Static analysis in GitHub Actions

The [minimal workflow](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/examples/github-actions/rea-analysis.yml) builds a small
JavaScript application, analyzes its files without executing them, and uploads
machine-readable results. It uses the existing CLI, not a separate GitHub Action
or an MCP client. It does not promise support for every REA provider.

## Run the example

1. Copy the example to `.github/workflows/rea-analysis.yml` in your repository and
   commit it to the default branch. No existing application or package manifest is
   needed for the self-contained demonstration.
2. Enable GitHub Actions if necessary. Select **REA static analysis example** in
   the Actions tab and choose **Run workflow**.
3. Download the `rea-analysis` artifact after the run. Its files are:

   | File              | Meaning                                                                                            |
   | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | `analysis.json`   | Original CLI JSON, including complete Evidence on success or the error report when one is emitted. |
   | `analysis.stderr` | Original diagnostics/progress; an empty file is normal when there are none.                        |
   | `exit-code.txt`   | Original analysis process exit code.                                                               |

The example pins Node.js 24.22.1, REA 6.7.0, and action commit revisions. It installs
REA into the runner's temporary directory rather than changing the application's
dependencies. This pins the tool version, not every transitive npm dependency;
use a reviewed, committed package lock and `npm ci` if your integration requires
that stronger dependency-reproducibility guarantee.

## Prerequisites and trust

The runner is GitHub-hosted Ubuntu 24.04 with Bash, npm, and `ps` from `procps`.
Other Linux images must supply `procps`; REA's supervised process controls use it.
This static JavaScript operation needs no Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, Java, browser,
Docker, GPU, external API key, or user-supplied GitHub secret. The workflow only
requests `contents: read`; artifact upload uses the runner's normal Actions
credentials.

Replace **Build a known artifact** with your reviewed build, and set
`ARTIFACT_PATH` to its application directory (relative to the checkout) or an ASAR.
The demonstration creates its own tiny application; it deliberately throws if
executed. REA reads it statically. Your replacement build itself can execute code:
review it separately and do not add untrusted pull-request builds to a privileged
`pull_request_target` workflow. The example is manually triggered, not an
untrusted-PR execution policy.

Reports can contain paths, URLs, source-derived facts, and caller-selected data.
Only analyze artifacts and publish reports you are authorized to share. Do not
rely on REA inferring secrets from their names. Review artifact access and
retention for your repository; the example retains reports for seven days.

## Failure, partial results, and unsupported capabilities

The analysis step captures stdout and stderr separately, records `$?`, and exits
with that same status. There is no `continue-on-error`, `|| true`, output filter,
or pipeline that could turn a failed analysis green. Before checkout or other
fallible steps, the workflow creates a fresh report directory under `RUNNER_TEMP`.
Analysis and upload both use that directory, never a checked-in `reports/rea` or
other workspace files. The upload step uses `always()` when that directory was
prepared, so available diagnostics survive an analysis failure. If installation
or the build failed before analysis began, it is empty and upload warns rather
than publishing stale results or inventing a successful result. Runner loss or
cancellation can still prevent upload.

`--json --full-output` selects a machine-readable envelope; it does **not** mean
that analysis was complete. A successful operation can retain partial analysis,
unknowns, and limitations. Exit zero is not a security verdict, proof of complete
coverage, or a policy gate for those findings. Inspect the saved Evidence and
coverage before making such a decision. See [output and exit status](cli.md#output-and-exit-status).

A nonzero exit can represent invalid input, unavailable tooling, an unsupported
host/capability, or another operation failure. Keep the original JSON error (when
emitted), stderr, and exit code, and use their category/message to diagnose it.
An early startup failure may leave `analysis.json` empty; do not parse that as
successful analysis. Select a supported operation or explicitly provision its
[documented prerequisites](installation.md); do not silently switch providers,
execute the artifact, or ignore the failure to obtain a green job.

To exercise the failure path, temporarily set `ARTIFACT_PATH` to
`build/missing-artifact` without changing the demo build. Analysis must fail,
`exit-code.txt` must be nonzero, and the available reports must still upload.
To exercise unsupported input, set `ARTIFACT_PATH` to `build/rea-ci-demo/index.js`:
this operation accepts an application directory or ASAR, not a single source file.
The retained JSON error has category `unsupported_target`; the step exits nonzero.
Restore the correct path before using the example normally.

To exercise partial analysis, append `export const broken = ;` to the demo's
JavaScript. REA 6.7.0 retains `data.normalized_result.statistics.parse_failures`
and an incomplete-coverage limitation while the operation can still exit zero.
Inspect those facts instead of treating process success as full coverage. The
report JSON and diagnostics remain unfiltered in all three cases.
